passage_flags: Factual check: Passage A matches Madrian & Shea (2001): April 1998 change at a large US firm; participation about 37% vs about 86% for comparable-tenure cohorts; biggest gains among young and low-income workers; low 3% default rate and money-market default fund (supports Passage B). 'Fewer than half' and 'close to ninety percent' are fair.

Factual check: Passage B's 'well-known program' is Thaler & Benartzi's Save More Tomorrow (savings rose from about 3.5% to about 13.6% in about 40 months), so 'more than tripled' holds. minor: that program was an opt-in commitment, not a default, though the passage's 'put that tendency to better use' wording is fair.

flags: minor: the next sentence ('matching contributions, investment choices... exactly as before') nearly states the purpose, so it reads close to a lookup
R034-01.notes: The sentence isolates the default as the only change, which rules out other causes of the participation jump. B, C and D have no support.

flags: answer cue: the key paraphrases the 'Because doing nothing is what most people do most of the time' clause just before 'never neutral'
overlap: the key gives away the core idea of R034-07's key (a default matters because people do not change it)
R034-02.notes: Direct causal 'because' clause. D contradicts it; A and C are unsupported.

R034-03.notes: Freedom is 'exercised' means it is used. 'Trained' and 'strengthened' lure students who think of physical exercise, but context makes C clear.

flags: minor: the quoted sentence names the general 'keeps people where it puts them' finding; contribution rates come in the next sentence. The stem's label is fair but slightly loose
R034-04.notes: 'Less loudly' means it got less publicity than the participation finding ('No one disputes...'). A, C and D are unsupported.

flags: answer cue: the key closely paraphrases 'not a flaw in the idea so much as the idea itself... That same tendency means...'
R034-05.notes: The paragraph says the drawback comes from the same inertia that makes defaults work. B contradicts 'decades... millions of accounts'; D contradicts 'No one disputes'; C is never explained. A standard function question, near the easy line.

R034-06.notes: Taking the increases from future raises means take-home pay never drops. Students must infer this because it is unstated. B contradicts 'few later bothered to stop them' (they could stop). A and C are unsupported.

flags: overlap: same core idea as R034-02 (key B) and R034-05; R034-02's key effectively previews this answer
R034-07.notes: A: 'doing nothing is what most people do' / 'choice of a default is never neutral'. B: 'people tend to stay with whatever requires no action'. A is the trap, but B says some workers saved less. C and D are clearly wrong, so this is near easy.

flags: minor: Passage A never explicitly says enrolled workers saved more. The 'impression' rests on 'accomplish what years of reminders and lectures about saving could not'. Defensible, but the key is implied rather than stated
R034-08.notes: B's finding of low default rates, with some saving less, undercuts the idea that higher participation meant more saving. A and B are A's claims that B accepts ('No one disputes'). C is a tempting trap because B discusses being 'held in place', but B never questions freedom to opt out.

flags: answer cue: the key nearly copies 'Some workers who would have joined on their own and chosen to save more ended up saving less', which makes it close to a lookup
minor: the stem ties B's claim to 'the study described in Passage A', but B speaks of 'the early studies' in general. A small attribution stretch
minor: partly overlaps R034-08 (both rest on the same contribution-rate sentence)
R034-09.notes: B and D name the groups A says were helped most, which is a plausible trap. A is not someone held at a low rate.
